6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d pick “Come Together.” The song opens in D minor, and the first harmonic move is from the tonic Dm to the minor fifth Am—the v chord. You can hear it in the opening vamp: the bass/guitar figure establishes D, then shifts to A minor before the first vocal settles in. Since the question asks for a tonic-to-minor-fifth jump at the start, that Dm–Am move is the key clue.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example is the A-major opening of Strawberry Fields
Forever.

The verse is in A major and the famous intro is laid out as a tonic → v
leap, A major → E minor.  The E minor is the diatonic minor fifth degree
of A major, the v chord, and the move is the I–v jump that is heard
right at the very start of the recording. The same I–v tonic-to-its-minor-
fifth move is the one that is normally quoted in the minor-key form as
i–v. The canonical minor-key Beatles illustration of that move is the
string opening of Eleanor Rigby, E minor i → B minor v, a tonic-to-minor-
fifth jump up a perfect fifth.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The effect you are describing is the famous piano opening of *A Day in the Life*.

The number is introduced in G major. The opening piano figure is stated on the tonic G major and the first real harmonic move of the statement is a hard leap down a diminished/minor 5th to the tritone. In the literature on the piece the move is normally described as the G–major tonic being answered by the bV/minor-5th area, the Gb/Db enharmonic complex that is heard as the G–D♭ tritone jump which is then resolved into the song’s E-minor/C-major orbit. 

The same tritone tonic→♭V jump is the one that is usually quoted as the textbook Beatles tritone opening and is the one most often cited for *I Am the Walrus* in the same family of analyses, the E-major tonic of the Walrus intro being answered by its ♭V/ tritone B♭ area. It is the A Day in the Life piano intro that is the canonical illustration of the tonic → minor-fifth/tritone chord jump in the Beatles catalogue.

The jump that is usually quoted in this connection is the tritone / ♭V opening that the
White Album opens with.

In E the first two harmonies of *I Am the Walrus* are

* E major = I
* B♭ major = ♭V

E → B♭ is a diminished / “minor” fifth in root movement, i.e. the tonic is left
and the next sonority is the chord whose root is a tritone above the tonic.  In
functional terms it is the familiar I – ♭V/I – v jump that the group uses
again and again in its hard-rock moments – e.g. the I–v opening of the
A-major *Helter Skelter / I’m Only Sleeping* type of riff – and it is the
text-book Beatles illustration of a tonic-to-minor-fifth root leap.  That is
the tritone opening that is most often cited for *I Am the Walrus*, and in the
I–v diatonic sense the same class of opening is the I–v start of *Helter
Skelter*.

jump.

the best textbook i → v opening in the catalogue is

change is the move up a perfect fifth to its diatonic v, B minor,
E  →  Bm.  That is the tonic E minor to the minor fifth-degree chord B
minor that is first heard at the very start of the 1966 *Revolver*
number.

* Colleagues 1,2,3 describe the textbook Beatles tritone tonic → ♭V jump. Col1 and Col3 identify the Sgt. Col1 also notes the same family of analyses is often cited for I Am the Walrus. 
* Col2 is explicit for the White Album opener I Am the Walrus: first two harmonies E major = I, B♭ major = ♭V, E → B♭ as a diminished / “minor” fifth root movement, tritone tonic → ♭V. Col2 also notes the I–v hard-rock class is reused e.g. Helter Skelter.

Diatonic v reading – tonic to the fifth degree which happens to be minor:
* Col3 distinguishes a strict i→v quality. With that definition the canonical minor-key example is Eleanor Rigby: strings open E minor i, first real harmonic change to diatonic v B minor, E → Bm. Col5 repeats Eleanor Rigby as the canonical minor-key i→v illustration and adds Strawberry Fields Forever as I → v in major: A major → E minor, the diatonic minor fifth degree.

* Key / spelling of A Day in the Life opening is inconsistent in the round: Col1 says G major → G♭/D♭, Col3 says A major → E♭ major. The interval is tritone in either description.

* Eleanor Rigby Em → Bm is i → v, perfect fifth up, diatonic minor fifth degree.

Unresolved:
* Whether the question means a root movement of a minor fifth / tritone, i.e. I → ♭V, or a tonic move to the diatonic fifth-degree chord which is minor in quality, i.e. I → v / i → v. Current belief is leaning to the tritone interpretation as the usual colloquial “tonic to minor-fifth jump”. Interval / root-movement reading = tonic → root a minor/diminished fifth away, tritone, tonic → ♭V, destination chord is major.
* Canonical examples repeatedly cited: *I Am the Walrus* E major → B♭ major, E→B♭ diminished/minor-fifth root leap, White Album shop-window, cleanest two-chord start; *A Day in the Life* A major → E♭ major, Sgt. Pepper citation of same I–♭V class. Colleagues 1,2,3,5 treat this as the normal pop-theory use of “tonic to minor-fifth/tritone jump”. The destinations are major ♭V sonorities, not minor-quality triads.

Diatonic-quality reading = tonic → fifth degree in its minor quality, v / i→v, root motion a perfect fifth to a minor triad.
* *Eleanor Rigby* Em i → Bm v, string introduction, classic textbook minor-key i→v.
* *Strawberry Fields Forever* A major I → E minor v, major-key I→v analogue, now challenged as borrowed/modal minor v in a major key where diatonic fifth is E major.

Colleagues 1,2,3 now accept Come Together as the cleanest literal start under this reading, while still ranking Eleanor Rigby/Strawberry as classic textbook.

* The phrase is “minor fifth chord,” not “minor-fifth interval/flat five”. If taken literally the destination must be minor; ♭V examples are major, so they solve a different clue.

* Eleanor Rigby has the correct i→v relation but its B minor is embedded in a contrapuntal string texture rather than a bare two-chord vamp.
